A LIPSCHITZ INTEGER GRAPH WITHOUT
THREE-TERM ARITHMETIC PROGRESSIONS
JENSEN KOHLMEYER AND LIAM KRUER
ABSTRACT. We construct a strictly increasing function 𝐹 : N → Z whose graph contains no nontrivial
three-term arithmetic progression and whose successive differences lie in a specified set of sixteen positive
integers, all at most 125. Thus 𝐹 is 125-Lipschitz, giving an affirmative answer to Problem 15 in Green’s
collection. Equivalently, its difference sequence is an infinite word over a finite set of positive integers
with no additive square.
The construction starts with a four-uniform substitution on six letters. A bounded correction depend-
ing on the endpoint letter converts an equal-sum condition into equality of three endpoint letters. The
remaining obstruction is excluded by an invariant with 3 688 states. Division of the three indices by four
preserves the required error bounds, so strong induction extends the finite verification to all indices. We
give the complete construction, a short reproducible certificate computation, and a Lean formalization
whose finite checks are reduced in the kernel. The formal proof uses only the axioms permitted by the
pinned Green 15 challenge.
1. INTRODUCTION
We write N = { 0, 1, 2, . . .} . Green’s Problem 15 asks whether there is a Lipschitz function 𝐹 : N → Z
for which
Γ𝐹 = {( 𝑛, 𝐹 (𝑛)) : 𝑛 ∈ N} ⊆ Z2
contains no nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression [ 4, Problem 15]. For a graph of this form, the
required condition is
𝑖 + 𝑘 = 2 𝑗, 𝐹 (𝑖) + 𝐹 (𝑘) = 2𝐹 ( 𝑗) =⇒ 𝑖 = 𝑗 = 𝑘 . (1.1)
If 𝐹 is strictly increasing, this is also the absence of a double three-term progression in the sequence of
its values. Brown, Jungić and Poelstra [ 1] discuss this formulation and its relation to the additive-square
question associated with Brown and Freedman.
For comparison, Cassaigne, Currie, Schaeffer and Shallit [ 2] constructed an infinite word over
{ 0, 1, 3, 4} with no three consecutive blocks of the same length and sum. Taking partial sums gives a
Lipschitz graph without four-term progressions. The construction below excludes three-term progres-
sions.
Theorem 1.1. There is an explicitly defined function 𝐹 : N → Z such that 𝐹 (0) = 0, 𝐹 is strictly
increasing, and
𝐹 (𝑛 + 1) − 𝐹 (𝑛) ∈ D ( 𝑛 ∈ N),
D = { 1, 3, 4, 9, 20, 30, 39, 49, 80, 90, 96, 106, 117, 119, 120, 125} . (1.2)
Moreover, (1.1) holds. In particular, | 𝐹 (𝑛) − 𝐹 (𝑚)| ≤ 125| 𝑛 − 𝑚| for all 𝑚, 𝑛 ∈ N.

The proof separates the arithmetic encoding from the finite computation. The encoding forces equal

4. PROOF OF THE MAIN THEOREM
Proof of Theorem 1.1. Use the function 𝐹 in ( 2.2). Its value at zero and its increment, monotonicity,
and Lipschitz properties were established in Section 2. Suppose now that
𝑖 − 2 𝑗 + 𝑘 = 0, 𝐹 (𝑖) − 2𝐹 ( 𝑗) + 𝐹 (𝑘) = 0.
Lemma 2.2 gives 𝑆(𝑖) − 2𝑆( 𝑗) + 𝑆(𝑘) = 0 and 𝑢𝑖 = 𝑢 𝑗 = 𝑢𝑘. Since 𝐺 (𝑛) = 𝑆(𝑛) − 3𝑛,
𝐺 (𝑖) − 2𝐺 ( 𝑗) + 𝐺 (𝑘) = 𝑆(𝑖) − 2𝑆( 𝑗) + 𝑆(𝑘) − 3(𝑖 − 2 𝑗 + 𝑘) = 0.
Corollary 3.5 now yields 𝑖 = 𝑗 = 𝑘, as required. □
The difference word of Corollary 1.2 can also be generated directly by a substitution on its sixteen
integer symbols; the complete table appears in Appendix A . The value 125 is an explicit upper bound
for this construction. No assertion that it is the smallest possible Lipschitz constant is needed for the
theorem.

raise RuntimeError(”unexpected certificate counts”)
print(f”{len(seen)} states; {edges} retained transitions”)
The output is 3688 states; 19020 retained transitions . The raise statements are actual
checks, so the exclusion does not depend on whether Python assertions are enabled. This executable
computation is supplied for reproduction; the accompanying Lean certificate supplies kernel-checked
closure and exclusion.
